title: Why mixing helps: 2008
objectives: Quote what the Nifty 50 and gold did in 2008.
Use the three portfolios to show why mixing reduces the fall.
body_md:
Assets do not move together. That is the whole argument for mixing, and 2008 shows it clearly.

## The year

- Nifty 50: about −52%.
- Gold in rupees: about +27%.

## Three illustrative portfolios of ₹10 lakh

| Mix (equity / debt / gold) | Value after a 2008-type year |
|---|---|
| 100 / 0 / 0 | ≈ ₹4.8 L (−52%) |
| 60 / 30 / 10 | ≈ ₹7.4 L (−26%) |
| 40 / 50 / 10 | ≈ ₹8.5 L (−15%) |

Equity and gold use the 2008 index moves above; debt assumes +7% for illustration.

## What to take from it

The mixed portfolios still fell. They fell by much less, and that is the point: a smaller fall is easier for a client to sit through, and easier to recover from. The mix does not remove risk; it spreads the sources of risk so no single one can sink the goal.
example: A client who saw her ₹10 lakh fall to ₹4.8 lakh in 2008-type conditions sold at the bottom. The same client in a 60/30/10 mix would have seen about ₹7.4 lakh, and stayed invested.
say: In 2008 the Nifty fell about 52% while gold rose about 27%.
A mix still falls in a bad year; it just falls far less.
never: Gold and equity always move in opposite directions.

check.q: In 2008, roughly how did the Nifty 50 and gold in rupees move?
check.why: They moved in opposite directions, which is why mixing helps.

check.q: ₹10 lakh in a 60/30/10 mix after a 2008-type year is worth about…
check.why: About ₹7.4 L, against ₹4.8 L all in equity and ₹8.5 L in a 40/50/10 mix.

check.q: What is the correct conclusion from the 2008 illustration?
o: A mixed portfolio still falls, but by much less, so clients can stay invested
Gold always rises when equity falls
check.why: The mix spreads the sources of risk. The fall is smaller, and that is what makes it easier to hold and to recover.
